statement.p: Select the trigonometric identity you used in solving this problem.

hint.p: The integral involves \tan u and \sec u where the exponent of \sec u is even and positive. So we rewrite in order to have one copy of \sec^2(-11 x) for the derivative, and use a trigonometric identity to turn the remaining even powers of \sec(-11 x) into an expression of \tan^2(-11 x). Then use u-substitution with u= \tan(-11 x).

Thus the integral can be rewritten as \int 10\tan^{4}\mathopen{}\left(-11x\right)\sec^{4}\mathopen{}\left(-11x\right) \, dx = 10 \int \tan^4(-11 x) \sec^2(-11 x) \sec^2(-11 x) \, dx = 10 \int \tan^4(-11 x) \bigg( \tan^2(-11 x)+1 \bigg) \sec^2(-11 x) \, dx Now let u= \tan(-11 x).
Letting u= \tan(-11 x) means that du= -11 \sec^2(-11 x) \, dx, and thus dx= \frac{du}{-11\sec^2(-11 x)}.

solution.p: The integral involves \tan u and \sec u where the exponent of \sec u is even and positive. So we rewrite in order to have one copy of \sec^2(-11 x) for the derivative, and use a trigonometric identity to turn the remaining even powers of \sec(-11 x) into an expression of \tan^2(-11 x).

Then let u= \tan(-11 x), which means that du= -11 \sec^2(-11 x) \, dx, and thus dx= \frac{du}{-11\sec^2(-11 x)}. \begin{aligned} \int 10\tan^{4}\mathopen{}\left(-11x\right)\sec^{4}\mathopen{}\left(-11x\right) \, dx \amp = 10 \int \tan^4(-11 x) \sec^2(-11 x) \sec^2(-11 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 10 \int \tan^4(-11 x) \bigg( \tan^2(-11 x)+1 \bigg) \sec^2(-11 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 10 \int u^4\bigg( u^2+1 \bigg) \sec^2(-11 x) \frac{du}{-11\sec^2(-11 x)} \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{-11} \int u^4\bigg( u^2+1 \bigg) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{-11} \int \bigg( u^6+u^4 \bigg) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{-11} \bigg[\frac{ u^7}{7}+\frac{u^5}{5}\bigg]+C \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{-11} \bigg[\frac{ \tan^7(-11 x)}{7}+\frac{\tan^5(-11 x)}{5}\bigg]+C \end{aligned}
The correct trigonometric identity used is E.
